longForm.title: My Lai, 16 March 1968: The Massacre and the Cover-Up
longForm.excerpt: On 16 March 1968, soldiers of Charlie Company, 1st Battalion, 20th Infantry, killed between 347 and 504 unarmed Vietnamese civilians in the village of Mỹ Lai. No enemy combatants were found. One helicopter pilot tried to stop it. The Army covered it up for over a year.
paragraphs: On the morning of 16 March 1968, Charlie Company, 1st Battalion, 20th Infantry Regiment, 11th Infantry Brigade, landed by helicopter on the edge of the hamlet of Xom Lang in Son My village, Quang Ngai Province. The intelligence briefing they had received the previous evening, from Captain Ernest Medina, told them the area was a Viet Cong stronghold. They were told to expect contact with the 48th Local Force Viet Cong Battalion. They were told the civilians would be at the market by 0730. What they found when they arrived was a village of women, children, and old men preparing the morning meal. There was no 48th Battalion. There were no combatants. There were no weapons. Charlie Company killed everyone they found anyway.

The killing lasted approximately four hours. Soldiers moved through the hamlet in groups, shooting people in their homes, in irrigation ditches, in the open. Families were herded into groups and shot. Lieutenant William Calley, commanding 1st Platoon, ordered his men to gather approximately 70 to 80 villagers into an irrigation ditch and opened fire. When some of his men hesitated, Calley fired himself. The total number of dead has never been precisely established; estimates range from 347 (the Army's figure from the subsequent investigation) to 504 (as recorded by the Vietnamese government on a memorial at the site). No weapons were found. No enemy combatants were identified among the dead. The official initial report filed by the Americal Division described the operation as a military success in which 128 enemy combatants had been killed.

Warrant Officer Hugh Thompson Jr. was flying an OH-23 observation helicopter over the area during the operation. He saw the bodies. He saw soldiers killing civilians. He watched Lieutenant Calley's platoon order people into the ditch and shoot them. Thompson landed his helicopter between a group of fleeing civilians and a group of US soldiers who were pursuing them. He told his crew chief and gunner, Lawrence Colburn and Glenn Andreotta, to open fire on the American soldiers if they attempted to harm the civilians further. He radioed for helicopter gunships to land and extract the surviving civilians — approximately twelve people — to safety. He then flew to a bunker where several more civilians were sheltering and extracted them. Thompson filed a formal complaint with his chain of command that afternoon. He reported that he had witnessed the deliberate killing of unarmed Vietnamese civilians by US forces.

Thompson's report went into the system and produced no visible result. The Americal Division's initial report — 128 enemy killed in action, a significant success — stood. The Army conducted no serious investigation in the spring of 1968. The cover-up was sustained by the military bureaucracy not through a coordinated conspiracy but through the ordinary operation of institutional incentives: investigations that found wrongdoing required accountability, accountability was professionally damaging to everyone in the chain of command, and the chain of command had every reason to accept the official version. Calley's immediate superior, Captain Medina, submitted the falsified report. The brigade commander, Colonel Oran Henderson, conducted what he later described as an investigation and found nothing to report. The division commander, Major General Samuel Koster, endorsed the finding. The story of what had actually happened at My Lai on 16 March 1968 remained classified.

The cover-up broke through two channels simultaneously, and neither of them was the Army's. In March 1969, Vietnam veteran Ron Ridenhour — who had heard accounts of the massacre from other soldiers — wrote a detailed letter to the Secretary of Defense, the Secretary of the Army, the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs, and 23 members of Congress, describing what he had been told. The Army was forced to open a formal investigation. In November 1969, journalist Seymour Hersh, working independently and without knowledge of the Army's internal investigation, published the story through a small wire service after mainstream publications declined it. The combination of Ridenhour's letter and Hersh's reporting made the cover-up unsustainable. The photographs taken by Army photographer Ronald Haeberle — who had been embedded with Charlie Company that morning — were purchased by Life magazine and published alongside Hersh's follow-up reporting. The images of the irrigation ditch full of bodies appeared in living rooms across the United States in December 1969.

The Army's subsequent investigation, the Peers Commission, named for Lieutenant General William Peers who chaired it, concluded that a massacre had occurred, that it had been covered up through the chain of command, and that approximately 30 officers bore some responsibility for either participating in or concealing the killings. The commission's report documented the cover-up in detail. Fourteen officers were charged; all charges against all of them were eventually dismissed or ended in acquittals, with the sole exception of Lieutenant Calley. Calley was convicted of the premeditated murder of at least 22 civilians and sentenced to life imprisonment at hard labor. President Nixon ordered him released from prison to house arrest pending appeal three days after the conviction. Calley served three and a half years of house arrest before being paroled in 1974. No one else served any prison time for My Lai.

The question of how My Lai happened — what combination of training, institutional culture, combat stress, and command climate produced a company of ordinary American soldiers who killed hundreds of unarmed civilians — has occupied historians, psychologists, and military ethicists since 1969. The free-fire zone policies that designated large areas of Vietnam as cleared for killing anything that moved contributed. The body count metric, which created institutional pressure to produce enemy dead regardless of how they were produced, contributed. The specific command climate of the Americal Division, which had a higher rate of war crimes investigations than other divisions, contributed. The experience of Charlie Company in the weeks before My Lai — booby traps and mines that had killed and wounded soldiers without a conventional enemy they could fight — contributed. None of these factors, individually or combined, constitute an explanation that removes individual moral responsibility from William Calley or the soldiers who followed his orders and killed people in the ditch.

Hugh Thompson received no recognition for his actions at My Lai for nearly thirty years. The Army's institutional response to what he had reported was to investigate whether he had endangered his fellow soldiers by threatening to open fire on them. In 1998, Thompson and his crewmen Lawrence Colburn and Glenn Andreotta were awarded the Soldier's Medal for their actions on 16 March 1968. Andreotta had been killed in Vietnam three weeks after My Lai; his medal was awarded posthumously. Thompson testified before Congress in 1998 that he had been harassed and threatened after going public with his account, that he had received death threats, and that the Army had treated him as a traitor rather than as a soldier who had obeyed his conscience and the laws of war. He died in 2006. The memorial at My Lai lists 504 names.

shortForm.title: Hugh Thompson at My Lai: The Soldier Who Landed Between Them
shortForm.excerpt: On 16 March 1968, Warrant Officer Hugh Thompson landed his helicopter between American troops and Vietnamese civilians and ordered his crew to open fire on US soldiers if they continued killing. It took the Army 30 years to give him a medal for it.
paragraphs: Hugh Thompson was 24 years old and flying an OH-23 Raven observation helicopter over Quang Ngai Province on 16 March 1968. His job was to spot enemy activity and direct ground forces. What he spotted from 1,000 feet was American soldiers shooting unarmed civilians. He landed twice. The first time, he marked wounded Vietnamese civilians with smoke so medevac helicopters would pick them up, then watched a US officer walk over and shoot them instead. The second time, he put his aircraft down between a group of civilians running from US troops and the soldiers pursuing them. He told his crew — Lawrence Colburn on the M60 machine gun, Glenn Andreotta managing the radio — that if the Americans opened fire on the civilians, they were to return fire on the Americans. This was not a decision that required a long time to make.

Thompson then called in two UH-1 gunships and asked their pilots to land and extract the civilians to safety. The gunship pilots — whose names deserve to be recorded, and are not as well known as Thompson's — agreed and flew the civilians out. Thompson found a bunker with additional survivors and extracted them as well. He then filed a formal report with his chain of command describing what he had witnessed: the deliberate killing of unarmed Vietnamese civilians by soldiers of the 1st Battalion, 20th Infantry. His report reached brigade level and stopped. The Army accepted the official version, which described the operation as a successful engagement against the Viet Cong.

Thompson spent the next year and a half watching the story stay buried. When Seymour Hersh published his investigation in November 1969, Thompson cooperated and gave interviews. He received a harassment campaign, not recognition. The Army investigated whether he had endangered US soldiers by his threats. He continued to press for accountability through the 1970s and 1980s, largely without institutional support. In 1998, thirty years after My Lai, Thompson, Colburn, and Andreotta were awarded the Soldier's Medal. At the ceremony, Thompson said that what he had done was not heroic — that it was simply what the laws of war required and what any soldier should have done. He said he was ashamed it had taken thirty years for the Army to say so.

onThisDay.headline: Yorkist Forces Destroy the Lancastrian Army at the Battle of Tewkesbury
onThisDay.summary: On 4 May 1471, King Edward IV's Yorkist army defeated the Lancastrian forces under the Duke of Somerset at the Battle of Tewkesbury in Gloucestershire. The Lancastrian Prince of Wales, Edward of Westminster, was killed during or immediately after the battle — the last Lancastrian heir to the throne. Queen Margaret of Anjou was captured days later. The battle effectively ended the Lancastrian cause in the Wars of the Roses.
